KEY MESSAGE 1... 
Quiet and pleasantly mild conditions will continue for the
remainder of the afternoon and evening as surface high pressure
over New England gradually departs east. This will start to
strengthen the southeasterly pressure gradient between the high
and the remnant low of Isaias, so some gusts up to 20 or 25 mph
are possible by mid evening, especially where downsloping is
favored in a SE low-level flow set up from northern Cuyahoga 
County to northern Erie County, PA. Otherwise, clouds will just
continue to increase.

The main impacts from Isaias will occur tonight and Sunday as a
strong mid/upper trough progressing into the West Coast deepens
mid-level southwesterly flow across the central CONUS. This
mid-level jet will start to eject the remnants of Isaias ENE at
a pretty good clip. The remnant low is currently moving into
Middle Tennessee and will lift across West Virgina Sunday
afternoon before exiting the Mid Atlantic coast Sunday night. In
terms of winds, breezy conditions are still expected as the
pressure gradient tightens and an area of 35-40 knot 850-925 mb
winds moves overhead late tonight and Sunday morning. However, 
RAP forecast soundings show conditions becoming fairly saturated
rapidly after 06Z, and this combined with a slowly weakening
wind field will limit most gusts to around 30 mph. The exception
will be where the SE low-level flow set up leads to downsloping
from northern Cuyahoga County to northern Erie County, PA. This
will locally increase wind gusts, so gusts to 35-45 mph are
possible there. Winds will increase after 06Z, with peak gusts
in the 08 to 18Z Sunday window. Winds will turn N to NE behind
the departing low late Sunday afternoon and rapidly diminish. In
terms of rain, the shield of steady rain is still expected to
lift across the region tonight and Sunday morning, with
additional showers wrapping around the back side Sunday
afternoon. However, QPF is trending lower due to a slightly
farther SE track of the low and mid-level dry air wrapping
farther north. Some locally heavy convective banding is still
possible, especially along a KCAK to KYNG line, but most of the
rain will be light to moderate stratiform. There remains an
unusually high amount of QPF variability in HREF and RRFS
guidance and individual members, including run to run flips, so
confidence in exact rainfall amounts is lower than normal. The
overall trend has been lower, so used a blend of NBM and WPC for
the final QPF forecast which is a close compromise of HREF and
RRFS ensemble QPF. This gives a few tenths to 0.25 inch in NW 
Ohio, 0.50 to 0.75 inch in north central Ohio, and 0.75 to 1 
inch in NE Ohio (east of I-77) and NW PA. Probabilities for
locally higher amounts are greatest near that KCAK to KYNG line.
These rainfall amounts and low stream flows combined with drying
ground should prevent any flooding except for areas that may
have blocked drains or culverts. The showers will start to move
in from south to north after 03Z, with the steadiest rain in the
06Z to 15Z Sunday window. The rain will be more intermittent
Sunday afternoon as the low pulls away.

After drying out Sunday evening, it is possible to see some
additional scattered, light showers Sunday night as an inverted
surface trough and some low-level moisture hangs back across the
area. This is shown by a few HREF members, so added low POPS
Sunday night. Another showers will quickly end by Monday
morning.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
Broad mid/upper ridging will briefly flex over the eastern CONUS
Monday and Tuesday as the aforementioned western CONUS trough
evolves into a cut off low. This combined with surface high
pressure settling over the Mid Atlantic region will support deep
southerly flow and well above normal temperatures. Look for
highs to reach the 75 to 80 degree range in NW Ohio Monday and
upper 60s to low 70s in NE Ohio and NW PA. Most of the CWA will
see mid 70s to low 80s Tuesday. A shortwave dropping through the
central/eastern Great Lakes late Tuesday into Wednesday will
push a cold front into the region. This front is trending slower
as the cut off low over the West keeps mid/upper ridging in
place across the Tennessee Valley and Southeast CONUS. The front
should still manage to push through late Tuesday or Tuesday 
night before stalling near the Ohio Valley, so showers and
thunderstorms are possible ahead of the front. There will be
some instability ahead of the front to support thunder given the
warmth, but a later trend should limit any strong/severe
potential. Will need to watch for gusty winds though given
favorable shear.
